newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Lebed to fight for presidency after sacking.
newsitem.headline: Lebed to fight for presidency after sacking.

text.p: Sacked security chief Alexander Lebed on Friday began his fight for a political comeback, but won little early support for his declared intention of becoming Russia's next president.
The presidential newspaper Rossiskye Vesti greeted the dismissal with a gleeful pun on Lebed's name, which means swan.
"The swan has flown away," it said in a banner headline.

President Boris Yeltsin, preparing for bypass heart surgery next month, said on national television on Thursday that he was dismissing Lebed from his top Kremlin post for lack of team spirit and his naked ambition to become the next president.

Lebed, a blunt-speaking former paratroop general, had paid the price for antagonising his Kremlin colleagues during a power struggle which sharpened after Yeltsin said on September 5 that he was preparing to undergo heart surgery.
In typical gruff fashion, the laconic Lebed, 46, shrugged off his dismissal, saying he had been dumped because he refused to conform.
"I was a black sheep in the herd. It was only a matter of time before they sacked me. I am not part of their herd," he told a news conference, appealing to his supporters for calm.

The State Duma (lower house of parliament) was due on Friday to discuss the situation following Lebed's sacking. But Yeltsin's former security adviser can count on little support there. Many deputies oppose the peace deal he brokered in breakaway Chechnya last August.
Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov reacted cynically to Lebed's dismissal, making clear he had little love for the man who could draw away his electorate in a future poll.
"His 'romance' with Boris Yeltsin lasted only two or three months and it was a clear political bargain," Zyuganov said.
He added that Lebed owed his rise to media coverage, something the communists feels they were cheated out of during Russia's presidential election campaign.
Yeltsin brought Lebed into the Kremlin as secretary of the Security Council to help him beat Zyuganov in the July election runoff after Lebed came third in the first round with 11 million votes.
But since moving into the Kremlin, Lebed has faced strong resistance to further advancement from powerful rivals such as Yeltsin's chief of staff Anatoly Chubais.
"I was an obstacle to plans by Chubais to set up a regency. He wants to become president," said Lebed.
Lebed said he was sorry to have lost the job as Yeltsin's envoy in Chechnya and showed little hope that the peace process would now stay on track.
Officials, including Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, dismissed his warnings, but some of the liberal media shared Lebed's concern.
"Whatever your attitude to Alexander Lebed...his sacking will lower tension in Moscow. The question is what might happen in Chechnya as a result," said Nezavisimaya Gazeta.

Underlining his isolation, several key political figures rushed to back Yeltsin. "What happened was to be expected. The country's top officials have long been aware that something was going wrong," said Chernomyrdin.
Powerful Moscow mayor Yuri Luzhkov and even Defence Minister Igor Rodionov -- seen as Lebed's protege -- joined the chorus of criticism against Lebed.

Lebed is now out in the cold. But he can draw comfort from the example of Yeltsin himself who was in a similar predicament in 1987 when former Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev engineered his removal from the policy-making Soviet Politburo.
Yeltsin seemed then to be heading for political oblivion. But four years later he was in effective charge of the country.
